1:
Why the ark went to this town is answered two ways. Ellicott takes it as the nearest large city to Bethshemesh still in Israelite hands; and though neither a priestly nor a Levitical city it had kept something of an ancient sanctity — before the Hebrew invasion it had been a notable high place and a seat of Baal worship, which he thinks was taken into account. Wesley reasons from convenience: the hill was strong, and being high was visible at a distance, which mattered to men directing their prayers toward the ark — and for the same reason David afterwards placed it on Zion.

Whether the townsmen hesitated is put differently. Gill says they made no difficulty but gladly received it, since if they knew what had happened at Bethshemesh they knew it was owing not to the ark but to irreverent handling; and as theirs was no Levite city they must have had men from Bethshemesh to carry it. Clarke supposes they consulted Samuel first, and that his encouragement is why no such destruction fell on them. Henry draws the moral from the same fact: the judgments of God on those who profane his ordinances should not make us afraid of the ordinances, but of profaning them.

What was done to Eleazar divides them. Wesley denies flatly that they made him either Levite or priest, since in Israel men were not made but born such, and takes the sanctifying as a setting apart to the work; the son was preferred as younger, stronger and freer from domestic cares, and the office was to keep the place clean and guard it. Clarke agrees the word signifies no more than setting a man apart to take care of the ark. Ellicott disagrees at the root, holding it most likely that Abinadab was already a Levite, since Eleazar, Uzzah and Ahio are Levitical names in that family, and that Samuel, unnamed here but no doubt directing the business, would have sought a man of Levi for the trust. He quotes a striking description of the office, that Eleazar was constituted not priest but watchman at the grave of the ark, until the joyful resurrection to come.

How long the ark stayed is a small crux, and Wesley solves it. Gill reckons the stay at forty to fifty years, since it lasted until David had reigned seven years over Judah; Ellicott calls it the ark’s home for nearly fifty years; Clarke says only that the chapter covers at least twenty years, the dates of its events being unknown. Wesley points out that the text does not say the twenty years were the whole stay: the ark remained about forty, but twenty passed before Israel became sensible of their sin. He also explains why it never returned to Shiloh: either that place had been destroyed, or God would punish the people by keeping it in a private place near the Philistines, where the generality durst not come.

Ellicott makes the twenty silent years the making of Samuel. He hears sadness in the note of time and thinks we read Samuel’s own words; but he insists Israel did not begin to hunger for God only when the twenty years were over, since the whole period was a stern trial, the defeat at Aphek and the destruction of Shiloh having laid Israel at the feet of the Philistines, whose hold the return of the ark did not loosen. In those years Samuel must have laboured incessantly to wake the old worship, his boyhood dreams scattered; taught by adversity he saw that no bold stroke of a few gallant patriots could save the nation, but would only sink it lower. Keil and Delitzsch are concerned instead to deny that anything is missing between the two verses, arguing that the clauses are joined and carry one closely connected thought, against a scholar who found a gap there.
3:
Where Samuel had been is asked at once. Henry says we may well wonder what he was doing all this while, since he has not been named for three chapters, and answers that his labours are not mentioned until their fruit appears; perceiving the people beginning to lament after the Lord, he struck while the iron was hot. Clarke notes only that we have heard nothing of him since he served at the tabernacle, and that he was now grown and established as a prophet in the land. Gill and Wesley both take the preaching to have been done on circuit, Wesley adding that he mixed exhortation with his judicial work as he went.

The two names are read as classes rather than individuals. Clarke says they were not two particular deities but two genera of idols, one masculine and one feminine, both plural and standing for all their gods and goddesses. Ellicott agrees the plurals refer to the many images, identifies both as favourite Phoenician deities, and says they represented the productive power of nature and were worshipped through the East with a wild and wanton worship. Henry and Wesley single out the second: Henry because it was the best-beloved idol, from which he draws that true repentance strikes at the darling sin; Wesley because the neighbouring nations more eminently worshipped her, and he bids them put the idols out of their houses, where some keep them, and out of their hearts, where they still have an interest in many.

Ellicott alone sees how dangerous the reform was. What the prophet summoned unarmed and undisciplined Israel to was a desperate venture: they were at the mercy of long victorious foes who held the chief fortified places with garrisons, and he was challenging them to defy the most cherished institutions of their oppressors and turn from reverencing what Philistia held sacred and all-powerful. He knew what he urged would provoke a dangerous and most unequal contest, and that defeat would bring a ruin hitherto undreamed of; the question was whether they had faith to plunge into it. When the images were thrown down, he counts it not merely a religious act but an open rebellion against a warlike people who had ruled them with an iron rule.

The gathering is read as war and worship together. Keil and Delitzsch say the object of calling the people to Mizpeh was that the religious act performed there might serve as a consecration for battle. Clarke reaches it practically: this appears to have been an armed assembly, since Samuel knew an unarmed multitude could not safely be convened near the Philistines. Ellicott says the gathering belonged both to religion and to war, its first object being to assure the Lord that the heart of his people was his again, its second to implore restoration; and he explains the name, properly Mizpah, a common name for lofty places, meaning a watch-tower where an outlook could be kept. Gill fixes which Mizpeh is meant, the city on the borders of Judah and Benjamin and not the one beyond Jordan.

The poured-out water draws the finest suggestion in the chapter. Henry takes it for humiliation and sorrow, the people pouring out their hearts in repentance and making public confession, giving glory to God and taking shame to themselves. Ellicott presses further: to a people trained to watch the meaning of symbols, the pouring out of water before the Lord signified the whole inner life poured out before him, and the fasting the sinner bowed down in grief. He then asks whether the strange custom heard of in later days, when the high priest filled a golden vessel with the waters of Siloam and poured it out silently before the Lord, may not have been the record of one of the holiest memories of the people — their reconciliation with their God-Friend at Mizpeh.
6:
Clarke admits at once that it is not easy to know what the poured water means. He notes that libation was a religious ordinance among the Hebrews and most other nations, the Greeks and Romans using not only water but wine, milk, honey and blood, and names six classical authors for it; then he gives the Aramaic paraphrase, that they poured out their hearts in penitence as waters before the Lord, and supports it with four scriptural parallels, ending with Hannah pouring out her soul. Keil and Delitzsch take the same paraphrase to be on the whole correct, and add the confession implied in it: behold, we are before thee like water poured out.

Wesley alone reads it the other way about. The pouring is an external sign by which they testified their own filthiness and need of washing by the grace and Spirit of God and the blood of the covenant, as well as their desire to pour out their hearts in true repentance; where the others find only confession, he finds cleansing too. He also glosses before the Lord as the public assembly, where God is in a special manner present.

What Samuel was doing there is put three ways. Clarke says he gave them ordinances, heard and redressed grievances, and taught them how to be reconciled to God, coining a phrase for the occasion: the assembly was held for purposes at once religious, political and military. Wesley takes judging as governing, reforming abuses, seeing the laws observed and wilful transgressions punished. Ellicott makes it a matter of public standing: for a quarter of a century Samuel had been the principal person among the people and had long exercised a judge’s functions, but the tribes were scattered and their fortresses in enemy hands, so that in this first general assembly the rank he had long really filled is at last publicly acknowledged.

The Philistine advance is read as a lesson in both directions. Henry notes they had no just cause for suspicion, and adds the shrewd remark that those who seek to do mischief to others will be forward to imagine that others design mischief to them. He then draws the double moral: evil sometimes seems to come out of good, since a meeting for repentance brought trouble and may have tempted them to blame Samuel; but good is at length brought out of that evil, for they could never have been threatened more seasonably nor better prepared to receive the enemy, and the Philistines could not have acted more impolitely for themselves. Wesley states the first half as a rule: when sinners begin to repent and reform they must expect Satan to muster all his forces against them. Ellicott finds the attack entirely predictable, since the sudden destruction of the idol shrines, followed at once by a vast assembly in so conspicuous a place, would naturally rouse the ruling nation.

Ellicott writes the crisis as a scene. The Israelites, unarmed or poorly armed, watch the advancing host from the heights and remember how, when Moses prayed, the Angel of his presence saved them — and they have with them a seer equal to Moses. Samuel offers hurriedly, the time being short, and, Ellicott concedes, with rites somewhat different from those enjoined in the law; and while the imploring cry is still going up and the smoke of the lamb still ascending, the first line of the Philistines appears on the topmost slope. Then the storm breaks, probably beating in their faces, and the tribes charge. Gill notes that Israel applied to Samuel not as general but as prophet, believing his prayers of more avail than any army; and Wesley turns the request into the type of a greater intercession, since he who receives Christ as lawgiver and judge need not doubt his interest in it, Christ never ceasing to appear in the presence of God for us.
9:
That Samuel sacrificed at all needs explaining, and two explain it differently. Clarke grants he was not a priest, and offers a choice: either he offered it himself, or he had Eleazar offer it and may still be said to have done it, since he who procures a thing done may be said to do it; and the failure to sacrifice at the tabernacle was justified by necessity, neither tabernacle nor ark being at hand. Gill reports a Jewish suggestion that he acted through a priest, being only a Levite, but prefers to say that as a prophet in an extraordinary case he might do it himself, as Gideon did, and offer it away from Shiloh, now destroyed, so that persons and places for sacrifice were dispensed with. Both note the lamb must have been eight days old to be lawful.

Two place-names defeat everybody. Of Beth-car, Clarke gives only the forms in three versions, Keil and Delitzsch say the site has not been discovered, and Ellicott glosses it house of the lamb, or as some render it house of the field, supposing a Philistine fortress where the beaten host could rally. Of Shen they do better. Keil and Delitzsch note the word means a tooth and seems to indicate a projecting point of rock; and Ellicott makes the same point with a modern parallel, that the name answers to the French dent, a favourite name for a peak in the Alps and Pyrenees.

The memorial stone is read carefully by Wesley. It was a rude unpolished stone, which the law against images did not forbid, there being no danger of worshipping it and it being set up only as a monument; and he notices what the others pass over, that the victory was won in the very place where Israel had suffered their earlier fatal loss. He presses the word hitherto as deliberately guarded: God has begun to help us, though not completely to deliver us, and by that wary expression Samuel excites both their thankfulness for mercy received and their care to please him, that he might deliver them effectually.

That the Philistines came no more is qualified in the same direction by two. Keil and Delitzsch say the limitation is implied in the context, since the next clause, that the hand of the Lord was against them all Samuel’s days, shows they attempted to recover their supremacy but could effect nothing; and they add that Saul’s battles fall within the days of Samuel, who died only a few years before him. Wesley says the same more simply, that they came no more with a great host but only with straggling parties and garrisons, and that all the days of Samuel means while he was sole judge, for under Saul they did come.

Ellicott makes the victory a turning point in the constitution of Israel. It was no mere solitary success but the sign of a new spirit which animated the nation through Samuel’s life and the reigns of the great kings after him: the petty jealousies gave place to a desire for unity, so that men aimed no longer at the glory of Judah or Ephraim but of Israel. More than that, the pure religion was no longer confided solely to the tribe of Levi, which had shown itself unworthy; the Levites still ministered and the house of Aaron still wore the high priest’s robe, but in religious matters the power of the priestly tribe was never again supreme, and from Samuel’s day a new order, that of the prophets, was acknowledged as the regular medium of communication. Henry says it devotionally: Samuel was a protector and deliverer not by dint of sword like Gideon nor by strength of arm like Samson, but by the power of prayer and a work of reformation — religion and piety being the best securities of a nation.
14:
How the cities came back is a small puzzle. Gill points out that no campaign is recorded: Israel made a demand after the victory, and the Philistines were so intimidated that they quietly surrendered them. Clarke supposes the recovery gradual, spread over several years rather than done in a day. On the phrase from Ekron even unto Gath, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree against the obvious reading: Keil takes the limits as exclusive, Israel receiving back their own cities up to the Philistine border and not the two chief cities themselves, and Ellicott doubts whether these fell into Samuel’s hands at all, the words more probably marking the direction and extent of the recovery.

The peace with the Amorites is explained politically by Wesley, historically by the others. Wesley identifies them with the Canaanites, so called because they had been the most valiant of those nations and the first enemies Israel met, and says the peace was made so that Israel might be freer to oppose the Philistines, now the more potent enemy. Ellicott takes them for the most powerful of the old tribes, the note telling us that in these days of restoration the tribes of the interior submitted quietly to the conditions imposed at the conquest. Clarke says simply that the remaining Canaanites kept quiet once the Philistines were broken.

That Samuel judged all his life must be squared with Saul’s reign, and each does it differently. Gill has him judge under Saul, hearing causes and reforming abuses, and rejects the Jewish reckoning of thirteen years as too short. Wesley makes the office indestructible: Samuel did not cease to be judge, having been made so by a call Saul could not annul, and exercised it on great occasions though not ordinarily. Keil and Delitzsch date the judgeship from Mizpeh, the prophetic labours having begun at the death of Eli. Ellicott has him lay the office down voluntarily in Saul’s favour, while his influence and authority remained undiminished. Clarke does the arithmetic, reckoning a life of a hundred years and a judgeship of sixty, and adds the sharpest remark of the four: Samuel seems in many respects to have been considered the governor of the people, while Saul was only looked on as the general of the armies.

The three towns of the circuit are read in opposite directions. Clarke spreads them over the nation: at Bethel Ephraim and the northern parts could attend, at Gilgal Benjamin and those beyond Jordan had easy access, at Mizpeh he was within reach of Judah, Simeon and Gad. Ellicott observes that all three lie in the south, in Benjamin, and concludes the opposite — that Samuel’s power was chiefly exercised among the southern tribes. On that he builds a large claim: the religion of the Eternal was early corrupted in the north, and the restoration so much less marked there that when the strong hand of Solomon was removed a formal secession followed at once, and with it a rapid deterioration in faith and practice.

The altar at Ramah must be defended, and all three defend it alike. Wesley says the law obliging Israel to one place was for the present suspended, Shiloh being laid waste and no other place appointed, so that Samuel built where he lived as the patriarchs had done, and not only for his family but for the country that resorted to him. Clarke holds that the altar being duly consecrated the worship at it was strictly legal, Ramah being the seat of prophecy and the only altar of God in the land. Ellicott says the same, that he followed the patriarchs’ custom when there was no national sanctuary, the ark being in private custody with no priests or ritual attached; and he adds a conjecture the others do not, that the sacred vessels were probably saved from Shiloh by Samuel and kept by him at Ramah.
